record.original_question: Let the Euler constant gamma be gamma = lim_{n->infinity}((1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n) - ln n). Is gamma rational or irrational? Is gamma transcendental?

evidence.quote: The Euler constant γ is defined as lim_{n->infinity}((1+1/2+...+1/n)-ln n). It is an open problem whether γ is irrational or rational. The question about γ being transcendental is also an open problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define the Euler–Mascheroni constant by
$$\gamma \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k} \;-\; \ln n\right).$$
(The limit is known to exist and equals approximately $0.5772156649\ldots$)

(a) Determine whether $\gamma$ is rational or irrational.

(b) Determine whether $\gamma$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$ (that is, whether there exists a nonzero polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ with $P(\gamma)=0$).
artifact.status_search_result: The irrationality and transcendence of the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ remain famous open problems. No proof of either statement is currently known, although there exist conditional irrationality results and numerical computations of billions of digits.

status_evidence.title: Euler's constant - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is not known whether γ is rational or irrational, let alone whether it is algebraic or transcendental.
status_evidence.claim: Rationality/irrationality and transcendence of γ are open.
